column4: The section's dictionary note for the root ض-ح-و says it carries the sense of not hurrying; 79:29 brings out the earth's ضُحَاهَا after darkening its night, repeating the dawn-and-night scene behind the section's opening.
The section explicitly glosses the root س-ج-و as stillness and applies it to night. This verse calls night سَكَنًا, a settled time, while placing sun and moon in measured courses.
The section's gloss of night as stillness is made explicit here: God made night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ, for people to rest in it, and day for seeing.
This verse likewise says night was made لِيَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day made bright for sight. It repeats the settled-night scene that the section draws from 93:2.
The verse calls night a time لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day a time of sight, then names this as God's favor. It gives another direct formulation of the section's still-night image.
The verse makes night a covering, sleep a rest, and day a time of rising/spreading. It expands the section's quiet-night and dawn pairing into the body's rest and return to activity.
The verse names night as a time for rest and day as a time to seek God's bounty. It joins the section's settled night with its soft-giving and ease-in-living details.

The section's root ء-و-ي includes tenderness toward someone; Joseph here takes his brother إِلَيْهِ and tells him not to grieve over what the others did. The sheltering gesture makes that tenderness concrete.

The youths take refuge in the cave, أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, and ask God for mercy and right guidance. It repeats the section's sheltering-a-vulnerable-person image through the same refuge root it discusses.

The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, where their Lord will spread mercy and ease their affair. This gives the shelter image an explicit movement from protection to mercy.

The section's dictionary note for ق-ل-ي includes driving a flock away. Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا when elite listeners want the believers gone, directly reversing that expulsive action.

Noah repeats that he is not one to drive believers away. In its own exchange, this verse rejects the social exclusion the section's secondary flock-driving sense and its ban on hard treatment illuminate.

The verse describes oppressed men, women, and children calling for rescue from a town of wrongdoers. Their subjection gives a concrete human scene for the section's account of قهر as domination joined to humiliation.

The verse forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best manner until maturity and commands fair measure. It extends the section's ban on overpowering an orphan to safeguarding his material rights.
After Noah refuses to drive believers away in 11:29, he asks who could protect him from God if he did so. This verse contributes the accountability behind that refusal.

The leaders call Noah's followers “the lowliest” just before Noah refuses to drive believers away in 26:114. This verse supplies the status contempt that presses against the section's command not to put down the vulnerable.

The section's dictionary note for ع-ط-و describes an obedient, nonresisting camel and a pliant bow. This verse describes mounts made subservient and asks riders to remember God's favor when they settle on them.

The two women hold their flock back until the shepherds leave and explain that their father is old. This specific vulnerable-flock scene connects to the section's secondary account of driving a herd and its concern for a gentle response to someone in need.
After the women's explanation in 28:23, this verse says Moses watered for them and then withdrew to shade. Its own contribution is practical help for people whose need he has just heard.

The instruction is to argue with the People of the Book in the best manner, except those who act unjustly. It gives another explicit boundary for measured speech alongside the section's soft word to Pharaoh and its ban on rebuking the asker.
The verse forbids walking on earth with arrogance. This is a specific contrary gait to the section's dictionary gloss of ه-د-ي as calm, well-conducted walking.
For retaliation, the verse permits only equal measure and says patience is better. It sets a limit on the overpowering response that the section's account of قهر warns against.

The verse bounds retaliation for an injury by equivalence, then commends pardon and reconciliation. It clarifies the difference between just redress and the domineering, humiliating grip the section prohibits.

The verse warns the Prophet's wives not to soften their speech in a way that invites desire from a sick-hearted listener, while commanding an appropriate word. This is a contextual boundary on the section's soft-speech image, which is directed toward the vulnerable and even toward Pharaoh.
